key_insight: A personalized “normative twin” cardiac model can detect hidden patterns of heart-shape deviation that reveal clinically relevant risk beyond standard measures like ejection fraction and strain.
clinical_relevance: This approach may improve risk stratification, especially for atrial fibrillation in people with preserved ejection fraction, by identifying patients whose cardiac shape looks abnormal relative to their expected healthy profile.
method: Compared each person’s cardiac shape to an age-, sex-, and body-size-matched digital twin of expected healthy function.
Learned deviation phenotypes from two independent shape representations: a 128D statistical shape model and a 64D deep generative latent space.
Tested whether deviation scores improved prediction of future cardiovascular outcomes beyond conventional biomarkers and against noise controls.
evidence_signal: Across UK Biobank cohorts, deviation scores improved prediction of incident atrial fibrillation in preserved-EF participants (largest gain: ΔC up to +0.068; likelihood-ratio P = 3.3×10^-8), with a separate smaller signal for stroke in an independent representation, and the model generalized to an external healthy cohort.
watch_item: The findings are promising but need broader external validation and careful integration into clinical workflows because performance differed by outcome and representation.
paper_title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
